title: Why Does a Tooth Still Hurt Weeks After a Root Canal?
metaTitle: Tooth Still Hurts Weeks After a Root Canal? Causes
metaDescription: Tooth still hurting weeks after a root canal? Causes include a high bite, slow healing, a missed canal or re-infection. Learn when to see a dentist in Markham.
excerpt: A tooth that still hurts weeks after a root canal has several possible causes, from a high bite to a missed canal. Here is how to tell normal from concerning.
heroImageAlt: Person holding their cheek with discomfort in a tooth that was treated with a root canal weeks earlier.
bodyHtml:
A tooth that still hurts weeks after a root canal can be unsettling, but it does not always mean something has gone wrong. Possible explanations range from normal, slower-than-expected healing to a bite that sits a little too high, a missed canal, re-infection, or even pain referred from a nearby tooth. The key is to tell the difference between discomfort that is fading and pain that is persistent or worsening — and to have it checked if it is not settling.

What is normal after a root canal

Some tenderness in the days after treatment is expected, especially when biting, because the tissues around the root were inflamed before treatment and need time to calm down. For most people this soreness eases over several days to a couple of weeks. Mild, steadily improving discomfort usually falls within the normal range. The picture changes when pain lingers for weeks without improving, comes back after settling, or gets worse.

Why a tooth might still hurt weeks later

A bite that is slightly high

If the filling or temporary restoration sits a fraction too high, the tooth takes extra force every time you bite, which keeps it sore. This is common and often easily corrected with a quick bite adjustment.

Inflammation that is slow to settle

When the original infection was significant, the surrounding bone and ligament can take longer to heal, and tenderness may persist for a while even though the tooth is on the mend.

A missed or extra canal

Some teeth have complex anatomy with additional canals that are hard to find. If one was not fully cleaned, infection can persist and keep the tooth symptomatic.

Re-infection or a leaking restoration

If bacteria get back into the sealed canals — for example through a cracked or leaking restoration — symptoms can return. Completing the permanent restoration promptly helps prevent this.

A crack in the tooth

A fracture can cause ongoing pain on biting and can be difficult to detect. The outlook depends on where and how deep the crack is.

Referred pain

Sometimes the treated tooth has healed and the real source is a neighbouring tooth, the jaw joint, or muscle tension, with the pain only seeming to come from the treated tooth.

When to return to the dentist

Book a review if, weeks after treatment, you notice any of the following:

  • Pain that is not improving, or is getting worse.
  • Throbbing, or pain that wakes you at night.
  • Swelling of the gum, cheek, or face.
  • A gum bump near the tooth, or a bad taste.
  • Persistent pain when biting on that specific tooth.

Your dentist can examine the tooth, check your bite, and take an X-ray to find the cause. Depending on what they find, the fix might be as simple as adjusting the bite, or it might involve root canal retreatment information at Smile Dental Arts Centre if the canals need to be revisited.

Should pain really last for weeks?

Mild, improving tenderness can, especially after a stubborn infection. Pain that stays the same or worsens over weeks is a reason to be seen rather than to wait it out.

Does lingering pain mean the root canal failed?

Not necessarily. Many causes, such as a high bite, are straightforward to treat. Only an examination can identify what is actually going on.

Can I manage the discomfort while I wait for my appointment?

Many people find that avoiding chewing on that side, eating softer foods, and using over-the-counter pain relief as directed on the packaging helps in the short term. These measures manage symptoms but do not address the cause, so they are a bridge to being seen, not a substitute. If pain is severe, or swelling or fever develops, seek care sooner rather than waiting.

Getting it checked

If a treated tooth is still painful weeks on, it is worth an assessment rather than guesswork. Dr. Neda Kadivar, a general and family dentist with over 20 years of experience, can review the tooth and your bite at Smile Dental Arts Centre in Markham, Ontario, and advise on the next step.

This article is general information and not a substitute for professional dental advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always speak with a licensed dentist about your specific situation.
